attribution.title: Marble Skill Taxonomy (v1)
attribution.standards: Curriculum standards referenced by the taxonomy have their own upstream licences (see PROVENANCE.md in that repository).
attribution.note: This is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ages are approximate and the taxonomy is not written for learners with additional needs. Treat prerequisite links as a starting point and use professional judgement.

subject: Personal & Social Development

topics.ds: Express their own feelings appropriately using words rather than actions — saying 'I feel angry because...' instead of hitting, shouting, or withdrawing
e: Use an 'I feel ___ when ___' statement during a disagreement
Choose to tell an adult how they feel instead of acting out physically
Describe their feelings about a difficult situation using at least two emotion words
topics.p: When {{name}} is frustrated — say a sibling takes their toy — do they use words to say how they feel rather than snatching it back or crying?

topics.ds: Understand that everyone has feelings, that feelings change throughout the day, and that the same event can make different people feel different things
e: Give an example of a time their feelings changed during a single day
Explain why two children might feel differently about the same event
Recognise that feelings are temporary and can change
topics.p: If you and {{name}} watch the same film and you find it funny but {{name}} finds it scary, can they understand why you both felt differently?

topics.ds: Name and recognise basic emotions — happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, and surprised — in themselves and in others by looking at facial expressions and body language
e: Label at least five basic emotions from pictures or real situations
Match facial expressions to emotion words in a sorting activity
Say 'I feel ___' using a correct emotion word when asked about their own day
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a friend crying at a birthday party, can they tell you what that friend might be feeling and name the emotion?

topics.ds: Understand that feelings have causes — something happens (a trigger) and that makes us feel a certain way — and begin to identify what triggers their own emotions
e: Describe a trigger for at least three different emotions from their own experience
Complete 'I felt ___ because ___' sentences accurately
Identify what made a character in a story feel a particular way
topics.p: When {{name}} gets upset about something at school, can they explain to you what happened that made them feel that way?

topics.n: How Emotions Feel in Your Body
topics.ds: Understand the connection between emotions and the body — recognising physical signals like butterflies in the stomach (nervous), clenched fists (angry), racing heart (scared or excited), and tight shoulders (stressed)
e: Name at least three body sensations and match them to the emotions they signal
Notice a physical feeling in their own body and identify the emotion behind it
Explain why the body reacts physically when we have strong emotions
topics.p: Before a school performance or sports day, can {{name}} notice and tell you about the physical feelings in their body — like butterflies in their tummy — and connect them to being nervous or excited?

topics.ds: Use a wider vocabulary of emotion words beyond the basics — including frustrated, worried, anxious, embarrassed, jealous, proud, disappointed, grateful, and lonely — and distinguish between similar emotions
e: Use at least five emotion words beyond the basic six in everyday conversation
Explain the difference between two similar emotions such as angry and frustrated
Choose a precise emotion word that fits a described scenario
topics.p: If {{name}} doesn't get invited to a classmate's party, can they describe whether they feel disappointed, jealous, lonely, or a mix — rather than just saying 'sad'?

topics.ds: Recognise that people sometimes hide or mask their true feelings — smiling when they're actually sad, or saying 'I'm fine' when they're not — and understand why someone might do this
e: Give an example of a time someone might hide their feelings and explain why
Identify mismatches between someone's words and their body language
Explain that hiding feelings is common but that it's usually better to share with someone trusted
topics.p: If a friend at school says 'I'm fine' but looks upset and is being very quiet, can {{name}} recognise that the friend might not actually be fine?

topics.ds: Understand that emotions come in different intensities — from mild to strong — and that the same emotion can feel very different depending on how intense it is (e.g., annoyed → angry → furious, or nervous → anxious → panicked)
e: Place three related emotion words in order from mild to strong
Rate their own emotion on a simple scale (e.g., 1-5) in a real situation
Explain why recognising intensity matters for choosing how to respond
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between being a bit annoyed about losing a game and being truly furious — and explain that they're different levels of the same feeling?

topics.ds: Understand that emotional responses are shaped by personal experiences, culture, and context — the same situation triggers different emotions in different people because of their backgrounds and past experiences
e: Explain why two people might have very different emotional reactions to the same event
Give an example of how a past experience shaped someone's emotional response
Describe how cultural background might influence what makes someone feel proud or embarrassed
topics.p: If one child in {{name}}'s class gets very scared during a thunderstorm while others think it's exciting, can {{name}} understand that the scared child might have had a frightening experience with storms before?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own emotional patterns over time — noticing recurring triggers, understanding their typical responses, and recognising how their emotional awareness has grown
e: Identify a recurring emotional trigger and their typical response to it
Describe how their emotional understanding has changed compared to when they were younger
Set a personal goal related to emotional awareness, such as noticing when stress is building
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you something like 'I always get stressed before tests but I've learned that's normal for me' — showing they understand their own emotional patterns?

topics.ds: Understand how emotions influence thinking and decision-making — that strong feelings can cloud judgement, that we often make different choices when calm versus when upset, and that recognising this gives us more control
e: Give an example of a time a strong emotion led them or someone else to a poor decision
Explain the idea of 'cooling off' before making an important choice
Describe how the same situation looks different when you're calm versus upset
topics.p: If {{name}} sends an angry message to a friend during an argument and later regrets it, can they explain how their anger affected their decision and what they might do differently next time?

topics.ds: Understand that people can experience mixed or conflicting emotions at the same time — feeling excited and nervous about starting a new school, or happy for a friend who won but disappointed for yourself
e: Describe a personal situation where they felt two emotions simultaneously
Explain why mixed feelings are normal and not something to worry about
Identify mixed emotions in a character from a book or film
topics.p: When {{name}}'s best friend gets picked for the team and they don't, can {{name}} explain that they feel happy for their friend AND disappointed for themselves at the same time?

topics.ds: Understand how the amygdala triggers emotional responses and how the prefrontal cortex (still developing in adolescence) regulates them; explain why stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) affect thinking and memory; understand that the adolescent brain's dopamine system makes feelings more intense; distinguish between emotion regulation (managing feelings effectively) and emotion suppression (pushing feelings down, which is counterproductive); introduce cognitive reappraisal as a research-backed technique for changing how we interpret a situation
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain, in basic terms, why teenagers tend to feel emotions more intensely than adults — what's happening in the developing brain that makes feelings so powerful during adolescence, and what's the difference between managing a feeling and suppressing it?

topics.ds: Understand that adolescence involves active construction of identity, leading to emotional complexity around questions of 'who am I?'; explore the emotional dynamics of belonging to multiple groups simultaneously (family, peer group, cultural or religious identity); understand social comparison and its intensification through social media; recognise that identity is not fixed and that uncertainty about identity is normal, not a sign of failure; develop language for navigating emotions tied to group membership and personal values
topics.p: If {{name}} goes through a phase of feeling unsure about who they are or where they belong, can they explain why this kind of uncertainty is a completely normal and even necessary part of adolescence — not a sign that something is wrong?

topics.ds: Introduce Goleman's emotional intelligence model (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills); develop vocabulary for complex emotional states (ambivalence, ennui, schadenfreude, awe, nostalgia, cognitive dissonance); understand the evidence linking emotional intelligence to wellbeing, relationship quality, and long-term life outcomes; reflect on personal emotional growth over the secondary school years; explore the relationship between emotional literacy and mental health, and know when to seek professional support
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe a real situation where being aware of their own emotions — knowing what they were feeling and why — helped them handle a difficult moment better than if they had just reacted automatically?

topics.ds: Show kindness and care towards others in simple everyday ways — comforting a friend who is upset, helping someone who has dropped their things, sharing without being asked, and saying kind words
e: Spontaneously offer comfort to someone who is visibly upset
Help another person with a practical task without being asked
Use kind words to encourage or cheer up someone who is struggling
topics.p: If a younger child at school falls over in the playground, does {{name}} go over to help or comfort them without being told to by an adult?

topics.ds: Understand that other people have their own feelings and thoughts, and that these might be different from your own — a foundational awareness that not everyone sees or feels things the same way
e: State that other people can feel differently about the same thing
Give an example of a time someone felt differently from them about the same situation
Accept another child's feeling as valid even when it differs from their own
topics.p: If {{name}} loves dogs but their friend is scared of dogs, can {{name}} understand that their friend's fear is real even though they don't feel it themselves?

topics.ds: Notice and appreciate ways that people are similar to and different from each other — including appearance, family structures, languages spoken, foods eaten, and celebrations observed — and understand that differences make communities interesting
e: Name several ways people in their class or community are different from each other
Describe at least one thing they have learned from someone who is different from them
Express a positive attitude about differences rather than judging them
topics.p: Can {{name}} talk positively about how families in their class are different — some have two mums, some speak another language at home, some celebrate different holidays — and see this as interesting rather than strange?

topics.ds: Know and use the key vocabulary for understanding others — empathy, perspective, kind, fair, community, similar, different, and care — and understand that these words describe real habits of thinking and feeling
e: Use the word 'empathy' correctly and distinguish it from 'sympathy' — e.g. 'Empathy means I try to feel what they feel'
Explain what 'perspective' and 'point of view' mean and demonstrate by describing how two people might see the same event differently
Use words like 'community', 'belonging', and 'inclusion' accurately when talking about their school or neighbourhood
topics.p: When {{name}} sees someone who seems sad or left out, can they describe what that person might be feeling using words like 'empathy' or 'perspective' — showing they're thinking about the other person, not just themselves?

topics.ds: Understand that people's lives and experiences can be very different from their own — that some children face challenges like disability, poverty, family difficulties, or being new to a country — and develop compassion rather than judgement
e: Describe at least two ways another child's life experience might differ significantly from their own
Explain why it's important not to judge someone based on their circumstances
Suggest a kind action they could take to help someone facing a difficult situation
topics.p: If a new child joins {{name}}'s class who doesn't speak much English or whose family situation is very different, does {{name}} show understanding and try to include them rather than avoiding them?

topics.ds: Understand what fairness means and why it matters — recognising that fair doesn't always mean equal (everyone getting the same) but can mean equitable (everyone getting what they need), and applying this understanding in group situations
e: Explain the difference between treating everyone the same and treating everyone fairly
Give an example of a situation where equal treatment wouldn't be fair
Apply fairness thinking when sharing resources or making group decisions
topics.p: If a child with a broken arm gets extra time to finish a task at school, can {{name}} explain why that's fair even though other children don't get extra time?

topics.n: Seeing Someone Else's Point of View
topics.ds: Practise perspective-taking by imagining how someone else might feel in a given situation — using prompts like 'How would you feel if that happened to you?' and applying this when reading stories or during real interactions
e: Describe how a character in a story feels and give reasons based on the plot
Predict how another child would feel in a described scenario
Use perspective-taking during a real disagreement to understand the other person's view
topics.p: When reading a story together, can {{name}} pause and explain how a character might be feeling and why — putting themselves in the character's shoes?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of social awareness — including stereotype, prejudice, discrimination, equality, equity, bias, compassion, and fairness — and understand what distinguishes these closely related concepts
e: Explain what 'stereotype' and 'prejudice' mean and give an example of each from everyday life
Use words like 'equality', 'equity', and 'bias' correctly when discussing a scenario — e.g. 'That's not equity because not everyone got what they needed'
Identify an example of discrimination in a story or news article and explain why it is unfair using the correct vocabulary
topics.p: If {{name}} hears a classmate say something that groups all people of a certain background together, can they explain why that's a stereotype and how it differs from a fact about an individual person?

topics.ds: Identify symbols and emblems important to Australia's identity and diversity — the Australian flag, the Aboriginal flag, the Torres Strait Islander flag, the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, the golden wattle and the national anthem — and what they represent
e: Identify the Australian flag, the Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag, and say where they are flown together (e.g. at schools or council buildings)
Describe what is shown on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms (a shield with state badges, held by a kangaroo and an emu) and name the golden wattle as the national floral emblem
Explain what one symbol represents (e.g. the Aboriginal flag's colours: black for the Aboriginal people, red for the earth and yellow for the sun)
topics.p: When {{name}} sees the Aboriginal flag, the Torres Strait Islander flag or the golden wattle, do they know what they are and what they stand for?

topics.ds: Describe how stereotypes can influence people's choices and actions, such as the toys, activities, sports, careers or clothes people choose or avoid
e: Give examples of how a stereotype might stop someone choosing an activity (e.g. 'only boys play football', 'only girls do dance')
Describe how toy or clothing ads aimed at boys or at girls can influence what children choose
Suggest how to make a choice based on interests and strengths rather than stereotypes
topics.p: Does {{name}} notice when ideas like 'that's a boys' toy' or 'girls don't play that' might stop someone from doing what they enjoy?

topics.ds: Describe how religious and cultural festivals (e.g. Easter, Christmas, Diwali, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year and Hanukkah) are celebrated in their community and country, and what each means to the people who celebrate it
e: Describe how one religious festival (e.g. Easter, Christmas, Eid al-Fitr or Diwali) is celebrated in their country and what it means to the people who celebrate it
Compare how two cultural or religious festivals are celebrated (e.g. food, gatherings, symbols and stories)
Explain why festivals from many cultures are celebrated in a diverse community, using a local example
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a festival like Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year or Christmas is celebrated, and what it means to the families who celebrate it?

topics.ds: Understand the impact of prejudice and discrimination on individuals and communities — that treating people unfairly because of their identity causes real harm — and act on their responsibility to stand against it by carrying out a strategy that values diversity and includes others in their school or community, then reflecting on its effect
e: Define prejudice and discrimination in their own words and describe the harm discrimination causes to the person experiencing it

Plan and carry out an inclusion action in their class, school or community (e.g. inviting a left-out classmate into a game, making a welcome sign in families' home languages, helping run an activity everyone can join)
Reflect on the effect of their action, using what people said or did in response, and suggest one way to improve it next time
topics.p: If {{name}} notices a child at school being left out for being different — new to the country, or using a wheelchair — have they actually done something to include them, like inviting them to play, and can they tell you how it went?

topics.ds: Recognise stereotypes — oversimplified beliefs about groups of people based on gender, race, age, or other characteristics — and understand that stereotypes are unfair because they ignore individual differences
e: Define what a stereotype is in their own words
Identify a common stereotype and explain why it is inaccurate
Challenge a stereotype they encounter by giving a counter-example
topics.p: If someone says 'boys don't cry' or 'girls aren't good at maths', can {{name}} explain why those statements are unfair stereotypes that don't apply to everyone?

topics.n: The world contains many cultures, traditions
topics.ds: Understand that the world contains many cultures, traditions, and belief systems, and that learning about others' perspectives enriches our own understanding — developing genuine curiosity about and respect for cultural diversity
e: Describe a cultural practice different from their own and explain what they find interesting about it
Ask respectful questions to learn about someone else's traditions or beliefs
Explain why understanding different cultures makes communities stronger
topics.p: Does {{name}} show genuine interest when learning about how families from different cultures celebrate, eat, or worship — asking questions respectfully rather than dismissing things that are unfamiliar?

topics.ds: Describe the diversity of First Nations Australians — Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples, each made up of many distinct groups — including the more than 250 languages spoken before colonisation and the languages spoken and being revived today; their social organisation (family and kinship, Elders, roles and responsibilities); and their continuous connections to Country/Place, recognising that Aboriginal peoples have lived on the Australian continent for more than 60,000 years and that Torres Strait Islander peoples have their own distinct histories and connections to their islands and seas
e: Explain that Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct peoples, each made up of many groups, and that more than 250 languages were spoken before colonisation, with many still spoken or being revived today
Describe, from an approved source, how social organisation is based on family and kinship, with Elders holding knowledge and responsibilities

Explain evidence that Aboriginal peoples have lived on the Australian continent for more than 60,000 years (e.g. archaeological sites and rock art), recognising that different places have different histories, and describe Torres Strait Islander peoples' distinct histories and continuing connections to their islands and seas
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct peoples with many groups and languages — and that Aboriginal peoples have lived on this continent for more than 60,000 years?

topics.ds: Describe the diversity of cultural, religious and social groups to which they and others in the community belong, and explain the importance of belonging to identity
e: Make an identity map showing the groups they belong to (e.g. family, cultural, religious, sporting, school and club groups)
Compare their groups with a classmate's and describe the diversity in the class
Explain how belonging to a group shapes who they are (e.g. language, traditions, friendships)
topics.p: Can {{name}} list the groups they belong to — family, culture, faith, sport, school — and explain how they help make them who they are?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own assumptions and biases — recognising that everyone carries unconscious assumptions about others, and that actively questioning these assumptions is an ongoing practice that leads to greater fairness and empathy
e: Describe a time they made an assumption about someone that turned out to be wrong
Explain what unconscious bias means in simple terms
Describe a strategy for checking their own assumptions, such as asking questions before judging
topics.p: Can {{name}} catch themselves making an assumption about someone — like assuming a quiet child is unfriendly — and then question whether that assumption is fair?

topics.ds: Investigate how the portrayal of societal roles and responsibilities (e.g. in ads, TV, books and games) can be influenced by gender stereotypes, and how these portrayals can shape expectations
e: Analyse a set of ads, book covers or TV clips and record how people of different genders are shown in roles such as caring, leadership, work and sport
Explain how repeated portrayals can shape people's expectations of who does certain jobs or responsibilities
Find or create a counter-example that challenges a gender stereotype about a role (e.g. a female engineer or a male nurse)
topics.p: When watching TV or ads, can {{name}} spot when jobs or chores are always shown being done by one gender — and explain how that might shape what people expect?

topics.ds: Move beyond 'treating everyone the same' to understand that structural advantages and disadvantages exist regardless of individual effort or intention; explore concrete examples of systemic inequality (educational attainment gaps, gender pay gap, representation in leadership); distinguish between individual prejudice and structural discrimination; understand intersectionality — how multiple aspects of identity interact; develop informed compassion rooted in evidence rather than pity; explore what being a genuine ally means in practice
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between treating everyone 'the same' and actually making things fair — and give a real example of a structural barrier that means two people starting in different positions face unequal opportunities even if they try equally hard?

topics.ds: Distinguish sympathy ('I feel sorry for you') from empathy ('I understand what you're experiencing'); develop active listening skills: reflecting, paraphrasing, asking open questions, resisting the urge to problem-solve too quickly; understand empathic curiosity as genuine interest in another person's inner world; practise being present for someone in distress without trying to fix or minimise their experience; understand vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue, and how empathetic people can protect their own wellbeing while staying present for others
topics.p: When a friend is going through something really difficult, can {{name}} describe what makes a listener genuinely helpful — and explain the difference between empathy and sympathy, using an example of something that sounds supportive but actually isn't?

topics.ds: Understand what it means to be a citizen in an interconnected world where decisions in one place affect people elsewhere; explore global issues (climate justice, forced migration, global health, poverty) through an empathy lens, distinguishing facts from value judgements; engage with the ethical tension between obligations to those close to us and obligations to distant strangers; introduce evidence-based giving and effective altruism as one framework for thinking about global responsibility; develop a personal, reasoned stance on global citizenship that acknowledges complexity
topics.p: When {{name}} reads about a crisis happening in another country, can they describe how they think about their own responsibility — and name one practical thing young people can genuinely do about large-scale problems rather than just feeling helpless?

topics.ds: Ask for help when they need it — from a friend, teacher, or family member — and understand that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness
e: Approach an appropriate person and ask for help clearly
Identify who to go to for different kinds of help (academic, emotional, practical)
Explain why asking for help is sensible rather than something to be embarrassed about
topics.p: If {{name}} is stuck on something at school or feeling worried about something, will they ask a teacher or friend for help rather than struggling in silence?

topics.ds: Seek permission respectfully before borrowing or touching other people's possessions or entering their personal space — asking clearly, waiting for the answer and accepting 'no'
e: Ask 'May I borrow your pencil?' or 'Can I sit next to you?' before taking or moving close, and wait for an answer
Accept a 'no' calmly and choose another option (e.g. ask someone else or wait for a turn)
Practise asking permission in role-plays (e.g. before hugging a friend or playing with someone's toy)
topics.p: Does {{name}} ask before borrowing a sibling's toy or giving a friend a hug — and accept it calmly if the answer is no?

topics.ds: Listen to others when they are speaking — looking at the speaker, waiting until they finish, and showing they have heard by responding to what was said rather than just talking about their own ideas
e: Face the speaker and maintain attention while someone else is talking
Wait until the other person has finished before responding
Respond to what was actually said rather than changing the subject to their own idea
topics.p: When a friend is telling {{name}} about their weekend, does {{name}} actually listen and ask questions about it — rather than immediately jumping in to talk about their own weekend?

topics.ds: Understand what makes someone a good friend — being kind, honest, reliable, and including others — and recognise behaviours that are not friendly, such as being bossy, leaving people out, or saying mean things
e: List at least four qualities of a good friend
Identify unfriendly behaviour in a story or real situation
Reflect on a time they were a good friend and explain what they did
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what makes a good friend and recognise when someone — including themselves — isn't being a good friend?

topics.ds: Give or deny permission respectfully when asked to share possessions or personal space, using clear words and body language, and know that it is OK to say no to sharing or touch that feels wrong
e: Say yes politely when happy to share (e.g. 'Yes, you can use it after me')
Say no clearly and kindly with a strong voice and matching body language (e.g. 'No thanks, I don't want a hug')
Practise responding to requests about personal space in role-plays and explain that everyone's body and space belong to them
topics.p: If a friend wants a hug or to play with {{name}}'s special toy, can {{name}} say yes or no clearly and kindly?

topics.ds: Take turns, share materials, and play cooperatively with others — understanding that group activities work better when everyone gets a fair go and that waiting for your turn is part of being a good friend
e: Take turns in a game or group activity without needing adult reminders
Share materials willingly during a shared task or playtime
Explain why taking turns makes games and group work more fun for everyone
topics.p: When {{name}} is playing a board game with friends or siblings, can they wait for their turn and share the pieces without grabbing or getting upset?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of working with others — cooperate, share, take turns, team, listen, agree, disagree respectfully, and include — and understand that these words describe habits that friendships and group work depend on
e: Use 'cooperate' and 'compromise' correctly — e.g. 'We cooperated by taking turns choosing the game'
Explain what 'active listening' means and demonstrate it: facing the speaker, not interrupting, responding to what was said
Use 'share', 'take turns', and 'include' to describe how they work with others in a group activity
topics.p: When {{name}} is working on something with a friend or sibling, can they use words like 'cooperate' or 'take turns' to describe what they're doing — and actually practise those things?

topics.ds: Resolve simple disagreements with peers by talking it through — explaining how they feel, listening to the other person's side, and finding a compromise or solution that both can accept
e: Explain their own point of view calmly during a disagreement
Listen to the other person's perspective without interrupting
Suggest a compromise or solution that addresses both sides
topics.p: If {{name}} and a friend disagree about which game to play at break time, can they talk it through and find a compromise — rather than one person always getting their way or the argument escalating?

topics.ds: Understand different roles people play in groups — leader, supporter, mediator, idea-generator — and recognise that effective groups need a mix of roles, not everyone trying to be the leader
e: Name at least three different roles people can play in a group
Identify their own preferred role and describe its strengths
Explain why groups work better when different people take different roles
topics.p: In a group project, can {{name}} recognise that they don't always have to be in charge — and that sometimes the group works better when they support someone else's idea rather than pushing their own?

topics.ds: Work effectively as part of a small group — contributing their own ideas, listening to others' ideas, taking on a fair share of the work, and supporting the group to reach a shared goal
e: Contribute at least one idea during a group discussion
Listen to and build on another group member's idea
Complete their assigned part of a group task on time
topics.p: When {{name}} has to do a group project at school, do they pull their weight — sharing ideas and doing their part — rather than sitting back or trying to take over?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of healthy communication and conflict — assertive, passive, aggressive, compromise, conflict, resolution, mediate, bystander, upstander, and peer pressure — and understand the difference between these contrasting approaches
e: Use 'assertive' correctly and distinguish it from 'aggressive' — e.g. 'Being assertive means saying what I need calmly'
Explain what 'conflict resolution' means and describe one strategy such as using 'I feel...' statements
Use words like 'negotiate', 'boundary', and 'respect' accurately in a discussion about friendships
topics.p: If {{name}} and a friend have a disagreement, can they describe it using words like 'conflict' or 'compromise' — and explain how assertive communication is different from aggressive or passive behaviour?

topics.ds: Understand that friendships change over time — that it's normal for friends to drift apart or for new friendships to form — and develop strategies for making new friends and handling friendship changes without feeling like something is wrong with them
e: Explain that friendships changing is normal and doesn't mean something is wrong
Describe a strategy for making new friends, such as joining a club or inviting someone to play
Talk about a friendship that changed and how they handled it
topics.p: If {{name}}'s best friend starts spending more time with someone else, can they handle it without falling apart — understanding that friendships shift and they can make new friends too?

topics.ds: Use assertive communication — expressing needs, opinions, and boundaries clearly and respectfully without being aggressive (pushy/demanding) or passive (giving in/staying silent) — including saying no when something doesn't feel right
e: Explain the difference between assertive, aggressive, and passive responses
Role-play saying no in a peer pressure scenario
Express a personal boundary clearly and respectfully in a real situation
topics.p: If friends want {{name}} to do something they're uncomfortable with — like excluding another child or breaking a rule — can {{name}} say 'I don't want to do that' firmly but politely?

topics.ds: Rehearse and refine strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission respectfully, reflecting on how a request or response went and improving it
e: Role-play asking for permission in two different situations and reflect on what made the request respectful
Role-play giving and denying permission with assertive words and body language, then refine the response after peer feedback
Describe what to do if their 'no' is not respected (e.g. repeat it, move away, tell a trusted adult)
topics.p: If you role-play with {{name}} — asking to borrow something, or someone asking them for something they don't want to give — can they ask and answer respectfully and improve it when you give them tips?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own role and behaviour in relationships — recognising patterns in how they interact with others, understanding what they contribute to friendships, and identifying areas where they could improve as a friend or team member
e: Identify a pattern in their own social behaviour, such as always wanting to lead or avoiding confrontation
Describe what they do well in relationships and one area they'd like to improve
Set a specific social goal, such as 'I will ask others for their ideas before sharing mine'
topics.p: Can {{name}} honestly reflect on their friendships and say something like 'I think I sometimes take over in group work and I'm trying to listen more' — showing awareness of their own social patterns?

topics.ds: Apply and rehearse help-seeking in online and offline situations: telling a trusted adult, keeping on telling until someone helps, using a personal network of trusted adults, and knowing help services and online reporting tools (e.g. Kids Helpline and the eSafety Commissioner in Australia). Know that it is never too late to tell and never the child's fault, and that a trusted adult helps report an unwanted picture without anyone saving or forwarding it
e: Identify a personal network of at least five trusted adults and what each could help with

Role-play telling a trusted adult about an online problem (e.g. a mean message or being sent an unwanted picture) and an offline problem, and explain that it is never their fault, even if they froze or couldn't say no
Identify a help service and an online reporting tool (e.g. Kids Helpline or the eSafety Commissioner in Australia) and practise how they would contact or use one with a trusted adult's help
topics.p: Does {{name}} have a list of trusted adults they could tell if something went wrong online or offline — and know about help services like Kids Helpline?

topics.ds: Describe situations when permission is required — borrowing things, touching or hugging, entering private spaces, taking or sharing photos and personal information online — and who can give it
e: Sort scenarios into 'needs permission' and 'doesn't' (e.g. borrowing a phone, posting a photo of a friend, hugging someone, opening a classmate's bag) and justify each choice
Explain why permission is needed before sharing someone else's photo or information online
Explain who can give permission in a situation (e.g. the owner of a possession, the person in a photo, a parent for a younger child)
topics.p: Does {{name}} know when they need to ask first — like before posting a photo of a friend or borrowing someone's phone?

topics.ds: Give and receive constructive feedback — telling someone what they did well and what could be improved in a way that is helpful rather than hurtful, and receiving feedback about their own work without becoming defensive
e: Give feedback that includes both a specific positive point and a constructive suggestion
Receive feedback about their own work without getting upset or dismissive
Explain why constructive feedback helps people improve
topics.p: If {{name}} reviews a classmate's story and finds mistakes, can they give feedback that's helpful — like 'I loved this part, and this bit could be clearer' — rather than just saying 'it's wrong'?

topics.ds: Mediate conflicts between others — helping two friends who are arguing by listening to both sides, helping them see each other's perspective, and guiding them toward a fair resolution
e: Listen to both sides of a conflict without taking sides initially
Help each person articulate their perspective to the other
Suggest a fair resolution or compromise that both parties can accept
topics.p: If two of {{name}}'s friends are arguing and both come to {{name}} for support, can {{name}} help them talk it out fairly rather than just taking one side?

topics.ds: Describe strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent — asking clearly, checking for a freely given 'yes', noticing non-verbal cues, accepting 'no' and knowing consent can be changed — and rehearse communicating their intentions effectively and respectfully
e: Describe what clear consent looks and sounds like, including that a 'yes' must be freely given and can be changed later
Rehearse asking for, giving and refusing consent in scenarios (e.g. sharing a photo, borrowing a device, physical contact in a game), using clear words and matching body language
Identify non-verbal cues that someone is uncomfortable (e.g. pulling away, going quiet) and explain why they mean stop and check
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that a real 'yes' has to be freely given and can be changed — and can they ask, agree or refuse clearly, like before sharing a photo of a friend?

topics.ds: Understand subtext, indirect communication, and social cues in adolescent peer groups; analyse the psychology of in-group and out-group dynamics and why belonging can come at the cost of exclusion; understand gossip as a social bonding and status mechanism, and its costs; develop strategies for navigating social hierarchies without compromising values; distinguish between assertiveness and aggression in peer settings; understand how to respond to exclusion — whether experiencing it or witnessing it
topics.p: When {{name}} senses tension or unspoken 'undercurrents' in a group of friends, can they describe what social cues they pick up on and explain the difference between being assertive and being aggressive when they choose to address it?

topics.ds: Understand how to have honest, direct conversations that address problems without attacking the person; apply the principles of non-violent communication (observation, feeling, need, request); understand the repair process after significant conflicts: taking responsibility without defensiveness, offering a genuine apology (without blame-shifting), and rebuilding trust through consistent behaviour over time; distinguish between a real apology and a face-saving 'sorry'; understand how friendships survive and deepen through navigated conflict rather than avoidance
topics.p: When {{name}} falls out seriously with a friend, can they describe what makes an apology actually repair a relationship — and what the difference is between a genuine apology and just saying sorry to end the awkwardness?

topics.ds: Distinguish different leadership styles (directive, democratic, servant, transformational) and understand when each is appropriate; understand that influence in a group comes with responsibility, and explore the difference between leading through inspiration versus coercion; practise inclusive leadership: actively creating space for quieter voices and diverse perspectives; understand the ethics of influence and the boundary between persuasion and manipulation; explore concepts of consent and coercion in peer relationships; reflect on what kind of influence they want to have in their communities
topics.p: If {{name}} were leading a group project where one person was dominating all the decisions, can they describe two different leadership approaches they could take and explain why the most authoritative person in a group isn't always the best leader?

topics.ds: Understand that actions have consequences — that what you choose to do affects both yourself and other people — and begin to think about what might happen before they act
e: Describe what happened as a consequence of a specific action they took
Predict what might happen if they choose a particular action before doing it
Explain that actions can have good or bad consequences for themselves and others
topics.p: Before {{name}} does something — like taking a toy from a sibling or running in the corridor — can they stop and think about what might happen as a result?

topics.ds: Recognise unsafe or uncomfortable situations and their body's early warning signs (e.g. butterflies in the tummy, a racing heart, sweaty hands), and tell the difference between safe surprises and unsafe secrets
e: Describe their body's early warning signs when they feel unsafe or worried (e.g. a racing heart or a funny tummy)
Sort scenarios into safe and unsafe situations and explain the clues (e.g. being asked to keep a secret that feels wrong, being touched in a way that feels uncomfortable)
Explain the difference between a surprise (fun and soon told) and an unsafe secret (makes you feel worried or uncomfortable), and that unsafe secrets should always be told
topics.p: Does {{name}} know how their body feels when something isn't safe — like a funny tummy — and the difference between a fun surprise and a secret they should tell you?

topics.ds: Keep themselves safe in everyday situations — knowing basic safety rules about roads, strangers, water, and the internet — and understanding who their trusted adults are and when to tell them something
e: State at least three basic safety rules and explain why each matters
Name their trusted adults and describe when they should tell them something
Demonstrate safe behaviour in a familiar everyday situation without being reminded
topics.p: Does {{name}} know their basic safety rules — like not going off with someone they don't know, looking both ways before crossing, and telling you if something online makes them uncomfortable?

topics.ds: Identify health and safety symbols, signs and messages in their community and what they tell people to do (e.g. poison and hazard symbols, hand-washing signs, sun-safe and 'no swimming' signs, the first aid cross)
e: Point to a poison or hazard symbol on a household product and say 'don't touch — tell an adult'
Find health and safety signs around school (e.g. hand-washing, first aid, exit or sun-safe signs) and say what each tells people to do
Match a community health message to the strategy it supports (e.g. a sun-safe poster to wearing a hat)
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a poison symbol on a bottle or a hand-washing sign, do they know what it means and what to do?

topics.ds: Understand that their body belongs to them, name body parts including private parts using correct terms, and tell necessary care apart from touching that is not OK: a parent, carer, doctor or nurse may sometimes need to help wash or check their private parts, but should explain why and ask if it's OK first; nobody else should touch or look at their private parts, and nobody should ever ask them to touch or look at someone else's private parts
e: Name body parts, including private parts, using the correct terms taught at school, and explain that private parts are the parts covered by underwear or swimwear
Sort simple examples into necessary care (e.g. a doctor checking a sore after explaining why and asking first) and touching that is not OK
Explain that nobody should ask them to touch or look at someone else's private parts, and that they should tell a trusted adult if anyone does
topics.p: Does {{name}} use the correct names for their body parts, and know that a doctor or carer who needs to check them should explain why and ask first — and that they should tell you if anyone else touches their private parts or asks them to touch someone else's?

topics.ds: Demonstrate and rehearse a protective response to unsafe situations: say 'no' clearly, get away, and tell a trusted adult — and keep telling until someone helps. Know that if someone hurts them or touches them in a way that is not OK, it is never their fault, even if they froze, couldn't say no or couldn't get away, and they can still tell
e: Role-play saying 'no' in a strong voice with matching body language in an unsafe scenario
Practise getting away to a safe place and naming who they would go to
Rehearse telling a trusted adult what happened, and explain that it is never their fault, even if they froze or couldn't say no or get away, and that they can keep telling until someone helps
topics.p: If something felt unsafe, does {{name}} know to say 'no', get away and tell a trusted adult — and that it's never their fault and they can still tell, even if they froze or couldn't say no?

topics.ds: Know the difference between right and wrong in familiar everyday situations — understanding basic rules about honesty, not hurting others, respecting others' property, and being fair — and choose to do the right thing even when it's harder
e: Identify the right and wrong choice in a simple moral scenario
Choose to be honest even when lying would avoid trouble
Explain why rules about not hurting others and being honest matter
topics.p: If {{name}} accidentally breaks something at a friend's house, do they tell the truth about it rather than hiding it or blaming someone else?

topics.ds: Understand why rules and agreements exist — that they help keep people safe, make things fair, and help groups work well together — and follow agreed rules willingly rather than only when being watched
e: Explain the reason behind at least two rules at home or school
Follow a rule consistently without needing to be reminded or monitored
Describe what would happen if nobody followed the rules in a specific context
topics.p: Does {{name}} follow the class rules or family agreements even when no adult is watching — not because they're scared of punishment but because they understand why the rules matter?

topics.n: Vocabulary: making decisions and keeping safe
topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of making decisions and keeping safe — choice, consequence, rule, safe, fair, honest, trusted adult, and right and wrong — and understand that naming these ideas clearly helps make better choices
e: Explain what 'consequence' means and give an example of a positive and a negative consequence of a choice
Use 'responsible' and 'safe' correctly when talking about everyday decisions — e.g. 'The responsible choice is to tell an adult'
Define 'rule' and 'fairness' and explain why rules exist using their own examples from school or home
topics.p: If {{name}} faces a situation where they need to make a choice — like whether to tell the truth about something that went wrong — can they talk through what might happen using words like 'consequence' and 'fair'?

topics.ds: Understand basic digital citizenship — being kind online, protecting personal information, recognising that people behind screens are real people with real feelings, and knowing what to do if something online makes them uncomfortable
e: State at least three rules for staying safe and being kind online
Explain why hurtful messages online are just as harmful as saying them in person
Describe what they should do if someone online makes them feel uncomfortable or asks for personal information
topics.p: When {{name}} is chatting with friends online or playing multiplayer games, do they treat people kindly and know not to share personal details like their address or school name?

topics.ds: Understand the bystander role — that when someone witnesses unkind or unfair behaviour, they have a choice: they can be a passive bystander (doing nothing), join in, or be an upstander (speaking up or getting help) — and develop the confidence to be an upstander
e: Explain the difference between a bystander and an upstander
Describe at least two safe actions an upstander can take
Give an example of a time they or someone they know stood up for someone else
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a group of children being mean to someone at school, do they have the courage to say something, walk away with the person being targeted, or tell a teacher — rather than just watching?

topics.ds: Investigate a range of health messages and practices in their community (posters, ads, school and family routines) and discuss their purposes
e: Collect three health messages from school or the community (e.g. a 'Slip, Slop, Slap' sun-safe poster, a hand-washing sign, a road safety ad) and say what each wants people to do
Discuss why a health practice matters (e.g. drinking water, wearing a helmet, brushing teeth) and who it protects
Create a simple poster giving a health message to younger children and explain its purpose
topics.p: When you pass a health poster or ad — like 'Slip, Slop, Slap' — can {{name}} tell you what it wants people to do and why?

topics.ds: Understand what bullying is — repeated behaviour intended to hurt someone, including physical, verbal, social (exclusion, spreading rumours), and cyberbullying — and know that it is always wrong and what to do if they experience or witness it
e: Define bullying and distinguish it from a one-off conflict
Name at least three forms of bullying including cyberbullying
Describe the steps they should take if they experience or witness bullying
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between a one-off argument and bullying, and do they know what to do if they see someone being bullied — rather than just ignoring it?

topics.ds: Use a simple decision-making process when faced with a choice — stopping to think, identifying the options, considering the consequences of each option, and then choosing — rather than acting impulsively
e: Describe at least two options when facing a decision
Predict a likely consequence for each option
Explain which option they chose and why, showing they considered the consequences
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a tricky choice — like whether to tell the teacher that a friend cheated — can they think through their options and the consequences rather than just reacting?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of ethics and citizenship — bullying, cyberbullying, bystander, upstander, peer pressure, digital citizenship, rights, responsibility, and ethical — and understand the distinctions between these closely related terms
e: Explain what 'ethics' means in their own words and give an example of an ethical dilemma
Use 'citizen', 'rights', and 'responsibilities' correctly — e.g. 'A citizen has the right to vote and the responsibility to follow laws'
Define 'consent' and 'integrity' and explain why they matter in relationships and online behaviour
topics.p: If {{name}} saw someone being treated unkindly online and you asked them about it, could they explain the difference between being a bystander and an upstander — and what 'digital citizenship' means?

topics.ds: Understand their rights and responsibilities as a member of a community — that everyone has a right to be treated with respect and to feel safe, and that with rights come responsibilities to treat others the same way
e: Name at least three rights that every child has (e.g., safety, education, respect)
Describe the responsibilities that go along with those rights
Give an example of how exercising their own rights responsibly supports the community
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that they have a right to feel safe at school AND a responsibility to help make school safe for others — understanding that rights and responsibilities go together?

topics.ds: Understand peer pressure — the influence friends and peers can have on your choices and behaviour — and develop strategies for resisting pressure to do something they know is wrong or that makes them uncomfortable
e: Define peer pressure in their own words and give a real-world example
Describe at least two strategies for resisting peer pressure, such as walking away or using humour
Explain why going along with something wrong to fit in usually makes things worse
topics.p: If {{name}}'s friends dare them to do something risky or unkind — like shoplifting a sweet or posting an embarrassing photo of someone — can they resist the pressure and explain why they won't do it?

topics.ds: Propose actions or responses to a community or environmental issue or challenge, considering the possible effects of each action on different people and places
e: Identify a local issue (e.g. litter at the school gate or a dangerous road crossing) and describe who is affected
Propose two possible actions and list a likely positive and negative effect of each for different groups
Choose the best action, explain why, and present it to someone who could act on it (e.g. the principal or a council member)
topics.p: If {{name}} notices a problem in your area — like litter or a dangerous crossing — can they suggest a couple of solutions and think about how each would affect different people?

topics.ds: Interpret the nature and intention of health information and messages (to inform, persuade or sell) and reflect on how they influence personal health decisions and behaviours
e: Compare a government health campaign (e.g. a sun-safety ad) with an ad for a sugary drink and explain the intention of each
Identify techniques a health message uses to influence people (e.g. facts, emotions, celebrities, catchy slogans)
Reflect on a health message that has influenced one of their own choices and explain how
topics.p: When {{name}} sees an ad for a sugary drink and a sun-safety campaign, can they explain what each is trying to get people to do — and whether an ad has ever changed what they chose?

topics.ds: Describe and apply protective behaviours in a range of online and offline situations (e.g. an unknown person messaging in a game, being asked to share a photo, feeling unsafe at a park or event), choosing safe responses: offline, say no, get away and tell; online, don't reply, block, and get a trusted adult's help to report. Never save, screenshot or forward a naked or sexual picture of a child; a trusted adult can help keep a safe record of an ordinary mean or threatening message
e: Identify warning signs in online and offline scenarios (e.g. a stranger asking for personal information, someone asking them to keep a secret, a game chat asking for photos)
Apply protective responses to scenarios: offline (say no, get away, tell) and online (don't reply, block, tell a trusted adult and get their help to report)

Explain what to do if they are sent or shown a naked or rude picture (don't save, screenshot or forward it; tell a trusted adult) and how a mean message is different (an adult can help keep a record of it to report)
topics.p: If someone they don't know messages {{name}} in a game, or sends a rude picture, do they know not to reply, save or share it, and to come to you so you can block and report it together — and, offline, to get away and tell you?

topics.ds: Identify who makes rules in the school and local community (e.g. the principal, school council, student representative council, families, local council), why rules are important and the consequences of rules not being followed
e: Name who makes three school or community rules (e.g. the principal sets the hat rule, the student council suggests playground rules, the council sets dog-leash rules)
Explain why a rule is important and what happens if it is not followed
Take part in making or reviewing a class rule and explain the process used
topics.p: Does {{name}} know who makes the rules at school and in your community — like the principal, the student council or the local council — and why they matter?

topics.ds: Explain why people participate within communities (e.g. to help others, to belong, for enjoyment, to improve a place) and how students can actively participate and contribute
e: Describe ways people participate in local communities (e.g. volunteering with the SES, Clean Up Australia Day, sporting clubs, festivals) and why they do it
Interview a volunteer or community member about why they take part
Plan and carry out one way they can contribute (e.g. a school garden roster or a litter clean-up) and reflect on its effect
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand why people volunteer or join clubs — and have they found a way to help out at school or in the community themselves?

topics.ds: Understand that ethical decisions are not always black and white — that sometimes there is no perfect answer and reasonable people can disagree — and practise weighing up competing values when making difficult choices
e: Describe a moral dilemma where both sides have valid points
Explain the values in tension (e.g., loyalty vs safety, honesty vs kindness)
Describe how they would make a decision in such a situation and justify their reasoning
topics.p: If {{name}}'s friend tells them a secret but the secret involves something dangerous, can {{name}} think through the tension between loyalty to their friend and the need to keep someone safe?

topics.ds: Evaluate the ethical dimensions of real-world issues they encounter — such as environmental responsibility, fairness in sport, digital ethics, or social justice — considering multiple perspectives and forming a reasoned personal position
e: Identify an ethical issue and describe at least two different perspectives on it
Explain which perspective they agree with most and give reasons for their position
Acknowledge that the other perspective has some validity even if they disagree
topics.p: Can {{name}} discuss a real issue — like whether it's fair that some children have more than others, or whether animals should be kept in zoos — considering different viewpoints and explaining their own position thoughtfully?

topics.ds: Distinguish rules from laws: laws apply to everyone in a state, territory or the nation and can be enforced by police and courts, while rules made by families, schools and clubs apply only to their members. At primary level, recognise that parliaments make statute laws (Acts) and that courts also develop common law through their decisions, and explain why laws are important and how they affect people's lives
e: Sort examples into rules (e.g. 'no hat, no play', a club uniform) and laws (e.g. road rules, wearing seatbelts) and explain that laws apply to everyone and can be enforced by police and courts
Explain that parliaments make statute laws (Acts) and that judges also develop common law when they decide cases in court
Describe how one law affects people's daily lives (e.g. bike helmet laws protect riders) and why it is important
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between a family or school rule and a law — like wearing a seatbelt — and that laws come from parliaments and from decisions in courts?

topics.ds: Describe the roles of local government (councils) and how members of the community use and contribute to local services
e: List services provided by the local council (e.g. rubbish collection, libraries, parks, local roads, pools) and say which ones their family uses
Explain that councillors are elected by the community and that councils are funded by rates and other money
Describe how community members contribute to local services (e.g. volunteering at the library, giving feedback, attending council meetings or paying rates)
topics.p: Does {{name}} know what your local council does — like bins, parks and libraries — and how people help by paying rates, volunteering or giving their ideas?

topics.ds: Analyse online and offline situations for risk — who is involved, warning signs, possible consequences and tricks people may use to gain trust (e.g. gifts, flattery, asking for secrecy) — and rehearse protective responses, knowing that if someone tricks or pressures a child it is never the child's fault, even if they went along with it at first or couldn't get away
e: Analyse an online scenario (e.g. a new online 'friend' offering gifts and asking to keep chats secret) and identify the warning signs and risks
Analyse an offline risky situation (e.g. being offered a lift by someone they don't know well, or being pressured by an older person) and plan a safe response
Rehearse protective responses for both scenarios using a personal safety plan and trusted adults, and explain that the child is never to blame and can tell at any time, even after going along with it
topics.p: Can {{name}} spot the warning signs if a new online 'friend' offers gifts and asks them to keep chats secret — and do they know it would never be their fault and they could tell you at any time, even if they'd already gone along with it?

topics.ds: Describe key values and features of Australia's democracy, including free and fair elections, the secret ballot and compulsory voting, and the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
e: Explain key democratic values such as freedom of speech, equality before the law and the rule of law
Describe how a federal or state election works (enrolling, compulsory voting, the secret ballot, counting votes) and run a class election with a secret ballot
Describe the roles and responsibilities of an elected representative (e.g. representing their electorate and helping to make laws)
topics.p: When there's an election, does {{name}} understand why voting is secret and compulsory in Australia, and what the person we elect is supposed to do?

topics.ds: Describe how citizens with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal, through actions such as petitions, campaigns, advocacy and volunteering
e: Describe how a group of citizens achieved a civic goal (e.g. a local petition for a pedestrian crossing, Clean Up Australia or a campaign for a new playground)
Identify the shared beliefs and values that brought the group together
Plan a class campaign for a civic goal, choosing methods such as a petition, a letter to a representative or an awareness poster
topics.p: Does {{name}} know how people work together to change things in the community — like starting a petition for a new crossing — and could they plan a campaign of their own?

topics.ds: Investigate different sources and types of health information — health professionals, product labels, government websites, apps and social media — judge their reliability and apply them to their own and others' health choices
e: Compare health information from a health professional or government website with a social media post on the same topic and explain which is more reliable and why
Read a food label (e.g. the nutrition information panel or the Health Star Rating in Australia) and use it to choose the healthier of two snacks
Use information from a reliable source to recommend a health choice for themselves or a family member and explain the evidence
topics.p: At the supermarket, can {{name}} use the food label to pick the healthier snack — and do they know which health websites or people to trust?

topics.ds: Describe the key institutions of Australia's system of government (the Parliament, the Governor-General, the Prime Minister and Cabinet, and the High Court), how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies
e: Describe the roles of the House of Representatives, the Senate, the Governor-General and the High Court

Explain features Australia takes from the Westminster system: the government is formed by the party or coalition that has the confidence (support) of the House of Representatives, which may be a minority government relying on crossbench members, and ministers must be members of Parliament
Explain values of Western democracies, such as freedom of speech and religion, equality and the rule of law, and how they appear in Australia
topics.p: When the news mentions Parliament, the Senate or the High Court, can {{name}} explain what each one does?

topics.ds: Distinguish between risk (decisions with known probabilities) and uncertainty (decisions with unknown outcomes); identify cognitive biases that distort risk assessment: availability heuristic (judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind), present bias (overvaluing the immediate over the future), optimism bias (underestimating personal risk), and groupthink; understand why adolescent brains are biologically calibrated toward higher risk tolerance; apply a structured decision-making framework to real choices; understand the role of personal values in decisions where facts alone cannot determine the answer
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why taking a risk isn't always irrational — and describe one cognitive bias that causes people to misjudge risk in their everyday decisions, such as why teenagers tend to underestimate certain dangers?

topics.ds: Describe the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government in Australia — federal, state/territory and local — and how some responsibilities are shared
e: Sort services by level of government (e.g. defence and passports: federal; schools, hospitals and police: state or territory; rubbish collection and parks: local)
Explain why some responsibilities are shared (e.g. roads or health) and give an example
Decide which level of government to contact about a community issue and explain why
topics.p: If there's a pothole on your street, a problem at the local hospital, or a passport to renew, does {{name}} know which level of government looks after each?

topics.ds: Understand the ethics of online identity and the importance of consistency between who you are online and offline; explain how recommendation algorithms and filter bubbles narrow information exposure; evaluate the psychology of misinformation: why it spreads, why smart people believe it, and how to apply source evaluation (lateral reading, checking evidence, recognising emotional manipulation); understand digital consent around sharing images or personal information; explore the ethics of AI, surveillance, and data privacy as they affect everyday life; reflect on responsible content creation and online influence
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a convincing claim shared on social media, can they describe their process for deciding whether to believe or share it — and explain why even intelligent people are regularly misled online?

topics.ds: Introduce the three main ethical frameworks: consequentialism (judge actions by outcomes and overall welfare), deontology (judge actions by adherence to rules and duties regardless of consequences), and virtue ethics (judge actions by the character they reflect); apply each framework to real-world moral dilemmas: climate responsibility, AI ethics, civil disobedience, wealth inequality, healthcare rationing; understand the strengths and limitations of each framework; develop the capacity for careful moral reasoning — the ability to think through ethical questions systematically rather than relying only on intuition or group opinion
topics.p: Can {{name}} take a real ethical dilemma — like whether it's ever right to break a rule to help someone — and explain how a consequentialist, a deontologist, and someone focused on virtue ethics would each think about it differently, and which approach they find most persuasive?

topics.ds: Investigate who they are — their likes, strengths, family background and what makes them special — and the important people in their world (family, carers, friends, teachers, community helpers)
e: Make an 'All about me' page showing their name, likes, favourite things and something they are good at
Name the important people in their world (e.g. family, carers, friends, teacher, a community helper) and say what each does for them
Say one way they are the same as a classmate and one way they are special
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you about themselves — what they like and are good at — and name the important people in their life and what each one does for them?

topics.ds: Notice what you are feeling and put a name to it — being able to label an emotion is the first step to understanding and managing it
e: emotional literacy research
Fostering Emotional Literacy in Young Children (HeadStart.gov)
emotion vocabulary development 4-11 years (PMC)
topics.p: When {{name}} seems upset, excited, or frustrated, can they stop and tell you what emotion they're feeling — even if they can't fully explain why?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of self-reflection — self-awareness, reflect, pattern, trigger, assumption, impact, perspective, and notice — and understand that having precise words for these inner experiences makes them easier to understand and talk about
e: Use words like 'reflect', 'pattern', and 'trigger' accurately when describing their own behaviour — e.g. 'I notice a pattern: I get frustrated when I rush'
Explain what 'self-awareness' means in their own words and give a personal example
Use the word 'perspective' correctly — e.g. 'From my perspective it felt unfair, but I can see theirs too'
topics.p: After a difficult moment — a falling-out with a friend or a frustrating task — can {{name}} talk about what happened using words like 'trigger' or 'reflect', showing they're thinking about their own reactions rather than just what the other person did?

topics.ds: Understand that feelings and actions are separate — you can feel something strongly without having to act on it straight away
e: emotion regulation development research
Effects of Age and Gender in Emotion Regulation (PMC 2020)
expressive control to emotion regulation (PMC)
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that feeling angry, scared, or jealous doesn't mean they have to act on it immediately — that there's a gap between the feeling and what they choose to do next?

topics.ds: Describe their own personal qualities (e.g. kind, brave, funny, curious) and those of others, and explain how these qualities contribute to developing who they are (their identity)
e: Describe three of their own personal qualities and give an example of when they showed each
Describe a positive quality of a classmate or family member and how it shows in what they do
Explain how one of their qualities helps make them who they are (e.g. 'I'm curious, so I love finding out about animals')
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what kind of person they are — kind, brave, curious — with an example, and say what they admire in someone else?

topics.ds: Notice patterns in your own reactions — 'I tend to respond like this when I'm tired, left out, or put on the spot'
e: middle childhood self-reliance in emotion regulation
7-year developmental shift in self-understanding research
topics.p: Has {{name}} ever noticed a pattern in how they react — for example, that they get more upset at certain times of day, or that a particular type of situation reliably triggers a strong feeling?

topics.ds: Investigate how experiences of success, challenge, setbacks and failure in different contexts (school, sport, friendships, hobbies) strengthen resilience and shape identity
e: Describe a success, a challenge and a setback from different parts of their life and what each taught them about themselves
Explain how getting through a challenge or setback changed how they see themselves (e.g. 'I now know I can keep going when things are hard')
Interview a family member, or read about a well-known person, and describe how a failure helped shape who they became
topics.p: Can {{name}} talk about something hard they got through — like a tough game or a test — and explain how it changed how they see themselves?

topics.ds: Reflect on how your behaviour lands on others — consider not just what you intended but what the actual impact was on the other person
e: Describe how something they said or did affected someone else — e.g. 'When I didn't include them, they looked upset'
Predict what might happen before acting — e.g. 'If I take the last one without asking, they'll feel it's unfair'
After a conflict, explain what they could have done differently and what effect that would have had
topics.p: Can {{name}} think about how something they said or did might have felt to the other person — not just what they meant by it, but what the impact actually was?

topics.ds: Notice when your first reading of a social situation might be wrong — your assumptions about why someone acted a certain way are not always facts
e: Pause before reacting to a classmate's behaviour and consider an alternative explanation — e.g. 'Maybe they bumped me by accident, not on purpose'
Describe a time they assumed the worst about someone's intention and later found out they were wrong
When told about an ambiguous social situation, suggest at least two possible reasons for the other person's behaviour instead of jumping to one conclusion
topics.p: If {{name}} felt sure someone was being unfair or unkind, could they pause and consider whether there might be another explanation for what happened?

topics.ds: Explain how identities can be influenced by people (family, friends, cultural and community groups, role models, media) and places (home, a family's Country/Place or homeland, community), and use strategies to create a positive self-identity
e: Create an identity map of the people and places that have influenced who they are, and explain one influence of each
Explain how a place (e.g. where they grew up, a family's Country/Place or homeland) can shape a person's identity, using an example
Describe strategies to build a positive self-identity (e.g. recognising strengths, positive self-talk, choosing supportive friends) and set one personal goal
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how the people and places in their life — family, friends, where they grew up — have shaped who they are, and name something that helps them feel good about themselves?

topics.ds: Reflect on your own growth over time — the things that challenge you now are not fixed, and noticing how you have already changed builds genuine self-knowledge
e: emotion vocabulary development continues to age 11 (PMC)
self-reflection importance in children research
topics.p: Can {{name}} look back over the past year or two and point to something they used to find really difficult that they now handle better — and explain what changed?

topics.ds: Understand that change is a normal part of life — such as starting school, getting a new teacher, a new baby arriving, or moving house — and identify simple strategies that help them cope with changes
e: Name at least two changes they have experienced and how they felt
Identify a person they can talk to when a change feels hard
Describe one strategy that helps them cope with change, such as keeping a familiar routine
topics.p: When something changes in {{name}}'s life — like getting a new teacher at school — can they talk about how it makes them feel and think of ways to help themselves adjust?

topics.ds: Understand that making mistakes is a normal part of learning and that everyone — including adults — makes mistakes, and begin to see mistakes as opportunities to learn rather than reasons to give up
e: Describe a time they made a mistake and what they learned from it
Respond to a mistake by trying again rather than giving up
Explain why mistakes help people learn
topics.p: If {{name}} gets an answer wrong in class or messes up during a game, do they bounce back and keep trying rather than shutting down or saying 'I can't do it'?

topics.ds: Wait for things they want without becoming very distressed — practising patience and delayed gratification in everyday situations like waiting their turn, waiting for a treat, or waiting for help
e: Wait for their turn in a game or activity without constant complaints
Describe what they do to help themselves wait, such as thinking about something else
Explain why sometimes we have to wait and that it is a skill they can practise
topics.p: If {{name}} has to wait their turn for something they really want — like a go on the iPad or being served dinner — can they wait without a big fuss?

topics.ds: Use simple calming strategies when feeling upset or overwhelmed — such as taking deep breaths, counting to ten, or going to a quiet space — and understand that these help the body and mind settle down
e: Demonstrate at least two calming strategies when prompted
Choose to use a calming strategy independently during a real upset
Explain in simple terms why calming down helps them think better
topics.p: When {{name}} gets really upset — say they lose a game or argue with a sibling — can they use a strategy like deep breaths to calm themselves down rather than staying in meltdown mode?

topics.ds: Know and use the key words for managing big feelings — calm, strategy, cope, settle, patience, overwhelmed, and breathe — and understand that having words for these ideas is the first step to using them
e: Use words like 'frustrated', 'anxious', 'overwhelmed', and 'disappointed' accurately to describe how they feel in difficult moments
Explain what 'calm down' strategies are in their own words and name at least two they have tried (e.g. deep breaths, counting, walking away)
Distinguish between similar feelings — e.g. explain the difference between being angry and being disappointed
